steps.title: Where this set work sits
steps.body:
This is the area of study **Vocal music**, alongside Queen's *Killer Queen*.

**The composer.** **Henry Purcell (1659–95)** was an **English Baroque** composer, widely regarded as one of the most influential English composers in the history of music. A pupil of **John Blow**, he **succeeded his teacher as organist at Westminster Abbey from 1679**, became **organist at the Chapel Royal in 1682**, and held **both posts simultaneously**. He began composing young and, in a short life — he **died at 36** — wrote a vast amount of sacred and secular music: **anthems, hymns, services, incidental music, operas** and instrumental music such as **trio sonatas**.

He is probably best known for the opera **Dido and Aeneas (1689)**. Other well-known works include the semi-operas **King Arthur (1691)**, **The Fairy Queen (1692)** — an adaptation of Shakespeare's *A Midsummer Night's Dream* — and **The Tempest (1695)**.

**The piece.** *Music for a While* is the **second of four movements** written as **incidental music** for **John Dryden's play based on the story of Sophocles' *Oedipus***. Dryden also wrote the libretti for *King Arthur* and *The Indian Queen*, and he and Purcell made a strong musical and dramatic pairing. Purcell set parts of the play to music in **1692**.

**The story.** The Oedipus legend is a tragic Greek myth in which the title character kills his father, marries his mother, and then dies gruesomely. This song features **Alecto**, one of the **Furies** — a goddess whose job was to punish those who had sinned, **specifically the crime of killing a parent**. She was a terrifying, Medusa-like creature with **snakes for hair, a dog's head, bat's wings, blood dripping from her eyes**, and **armed with a whip**.

**In this aria it is the music which calms Alecto**, until she **drops her whip** and the **snakes fall from her head** — which is exactly what the word-painting depicts.

steps.title: Performing forces
steps.body:
*Music for a While* was written for **voice — most usually a tenor — and continuo**.

**The edition you study** is scored for **soprano, harpsichord and bass viol**, and has been **transposed from the original key of C minor to A minor**.

**The harpsichord right hand** is an **elaborate realisation**: highly decorative and embellished with frequent **dotted rhythms** and ornamentation such as **upper and lower mordents, grace notes and appoggiaturas**. At the time this would have been **improvised by the player rather than notated** — the composer wrote a bass line and figures, and the performer filled in the harmony. Chords are frequently **arpeggiated**, or **spread rapidly from the lowest to the highest note**, as at **bar 13**.

**The harpsichord left hand plays the ground bass**, and the **bass viol plays it too**, doubling it.

**The bass viol** is a **bowed, fretted, stringed instrument** used in the **Renaissance and Baroque** periods. Although it resembles the modern cello, it differs in several ways:

- it generally has **six strings**, **tuned in fourths with a third in the middle** — **D, G, C, E, A, D** — and the seven-stringed version adds a **low A**
- a **flat** rather than curved **back**
- **sloped** rather than square **shoulders**
- **C** rather than **F holes**
- **frets**, which a cello does not have
- the player uses an **underhand** rather than overhand **bow grip**

steps.title: The ground bass
steps.body:
The piece follows a **ground bass** structure: a **short, recurring melodic pattern in the bass part** that acts as the **principal structural element**, while the melodic parts above it change. It is also known as a **basso ostinato**, and it was developed into forms such as the **Chaconne** and **Passacaglia**.

It was a common device in the **Baroque** period, and **Purcell is regarded as a master of the ground bass**, using it extensively. His best-known ground bass aria is **"Dido's Lament"** from *Dido and Aeneas*.

**Features of this ground bass:**

- It is **3 bars long**.
- It consists **entirely of quaver rhythms**.
- Its melodic shape is **arpeggio based**.
- It makes use of **semitone intervals**.
- It has a **rising line**, starting on **A** and moving up through **B, C, D, E** before **falling at the end of the phrase**.
- At the end of the ground there is a characteristic **fall of an octave**.
- The ground **sounds incomplete**, because it ends with **chord V** — but a sense of a **perfect cadence** is achieved with **chord I at the start of the next repetition**.

**Where it is heard.** The ground is heard **four and a half times in the tonic key** before it **begins to modulate in bar 14**, using **motifs from the original ground** rather than the ground itself. It **returns in the original key at bar 23, beat 3**, for a **three-bar reminder**. It **returns complete at bar 29** and is heard a **further three times** before the close.

**Looking forward.** Alongside the ground bass there is a sense of Purcell anticipating what became the **ternary *da capo* aria** structure, popular in operatic arias later in the Baroque period. This is seen at **bar 29**, where material from the opening is **reprised in identical form**, with only a slight extension to conclude the work.

steps.title: Text setting and word-painting
steps.body:
**Text setting.** The vocal line is **mainly syllabic**, following **speech rhythms** — one note per syllable. Against that:

- there are **paired slurrings**, for example in **bar 5** on the words *"for"* and *"a"*
- there are **melismatic moments**, for example **bar 10** on *"wond'ring"*
- there is an **extended melisma** in **bar 20** on *"eternal"*
- **repetition of text** is used, such as the word *"Music"* at the start, or *"drop"* in bar 23, sung **9 times**

**Word-painting** is the technique of writing music that reflects the **literal meaning** of a song. This aria contains many examples, and they are the heart of what makes it a set work:

- *"wond’ring"* at bar 10: a wistfully descending legato melisma, capturing the mood of the word.
- *"pains"* at bar 12: a dissonance, E in the voice against D in the bass — appropriately harsh for the word.
- *"eas’d"* at bars 13 to 14: dissonance then resolution, in a descending sequence, so the music itself is eased.
- *"free the dead"* at bars 16 to 17: the bright key of G major, with rising melodies.
- *"eternal"* at bar 20: a lengthy melisma on repetitive alternating notes, suggesting something everlasting.
- *"drop"* at bars 23 to 25: a descending pattern on the weak off-beat, sung nine times — representing **the snakes dropping from Alecto's head**.

**And overall**: the **predominantly minor key** suits the **sombre nature** of the play and the text.

steps.title: Melody
steps.body:
- The soprano line has a **range or compass of a ninth** — apart from the ornamental **G in bar 36** — from the lowest note of **E just above middle C** to **F just over an octave higher**.
- Much of the music is **conjunct** or **stepwise**.
- **Passing notes are frequent**. For example, the **E and C on beat 4 of bar 5** are **non-harmony notes**: they do not belong to the chord, but link notes that do.
- Any **leaps are small**, generally **no greater than a perfect fourth**, as at **bar 7**.
- **Rests are used to break up phrases**.
- There are some **descending sequences**, for example at **bar 20**.
- There is **extensive use of ornaments** in both the soprano line and the right hand of the harpsichord:
  - **trills**, for example bar 13
  - **appoggiaturas**, for example bar 35
  - **grace notes**, for example bar 6
  - **upper mordents**, for example bar 22
  - **lower mordents**, for example bar 1

The combination — mostly stepwise, small leaps, frequent ornament — is characteristic of **Baroque vocal writing**, where the decoration carries much of the expression.

steps.title: Tonality, harmony and texture
steps.body:
**Tonality.**

- The music is in **A minor**, coloured by a **Tierce de Picardie** — a major third in the final chord of a minor-key piece.
- The tonality is **sometimes ambiguous**, because the ground bass is **chromatic and non-diatonic**.
- The **central section modulates to closely related keys**, and **modulations are confirmed by perfect cadences**.

**Harmony.**

- Chords are **diatonic and functional**.
- **Perfect cadences** run from the **chord V at the end of the ground** to the **chord I at the start of the next playing** — for example bars 3 to 4. This is a **Ic–V–I cadential 6–4**.
- **Suspensions** are used **very occasionally**: there is a **4–3 suspension in bar 3, beat 4½**, in the harpsichord part.
- **Dissonances are infrequent**, but there is one on *"pains"* in **bar 12** — a **D in the bass against an E in the voice** — and on *"eas'd"* in **bars 13 to 14**, where dissonance is followed by resolution.
- Another type of dissonance is the **false relation**, seen in **bar 1**: an **F sharp in the ground bass** against an **F natural in the right hand of the harpsichord**. Strictly they are not adjacent, but they colour adjacent chords.

**Texture.** The texture is **melody and accompaniment**, also called **melody-dominated homophony**.

- The **accompaniment** is the **ground bass**, in the **harpsichord left hand** and the **bass viol**.
- The **harpsichord right hand** is an **elaborate realisation** that provides **some counterpoint with the vocal line**.

**Tempo, metre and rhythm.** There is **no tempo indication**, though a **slow** tempo would be appropriate. The metre is **4/4 quadruple time**. A wide variety of rhythms is used, but **quavers and semiquavers predominate**. **Dotted rhythms** appear sometimes in the vocal part, as at bar 10, and **more extensively in the harpsichord right hand**. There is **only occasional syncopation**, as at bar 20, and **off-beat rhythms**, as at bar 24. The **ground bass is presented entirely in quavers**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Explain the ground bass, do not just name it.** A top answer says it is **3 bars**, **entirely quavers**, **arpeggio based**, uses **semitone intervals**, **rises from A through B, C, D, E**, and ends with a **fall of an octave** onto **chord V** — so the perfect cadence completes **at the start of the next repetition**.

**Say what changes above the ground.** The point of a ground bass is **repetition below, variety above**. The vocal line and the harpsichord realisation are constantly new; that contrast is the answer to "how does Purcell keep it interesting?"

**Note that the ground is not continuous.** It breaks off to **modulate at bar 14**, returns for a **three-bar reminder at bar 23 beat 3**, and only comes back complete at **bar 29**. Saying it simply repeats throughout is wrong.

**Name the word, the bar and the device.** *"Drop"* sung **9 times** in a descending pattern on the **weak off-beat**, bars 23 to 25, depicting the **snakes falling from Alecto's head** — that is a complete word-painting answer. *"Eternal"* on a lengthy melisma, bar 20. *"Free the dead"* in the bright key of **G major**, bars 16 to 17.

**Use the right term for each dissonance.** The **false relation** in bar 1 is **F sharp in the ground against F natural in the harpsichord**. The clash on *"pains"* in bar 12 is a **dissonance**, D against E. The **4–3 suspension** is in bar 3. They are three different things.

**Be precise about the key.** The edition is in **A minor**, **transposed from Purcell's C minor**, and it is coloured by a **Tierce de Picardie**. The tonality is **sometimes ambiguous** because the ground is **chromatic and non-diatonic**.

**Mention the da capo foreshadowing.** The reprise of opening material at **bar 29**, in identical form with a slight extension, anticipates the **ternary da capo aria** that became standard later in the Baroque.

**Remember the realisation was improvised.** The harpsichord right hand as printed is an **editorial realisation**; at the time the player would have improvised it from a figured bass. That is a genuine Baroque performance-practice point.

- Area of study **Vocal music**. **Henry Purcell (1659–95)**, **English Baroque**, pupil of **John Blow**, organist at **Westminster Abbey** from 1679 and the **Chapel Royal** from 1682, died at **36**.
- Best known for **Dido and Aeneas (1689)**; also **King Arthur**, **The Fairy Queen**, **The Tempest**.
- *Music for a While* is the **second of four movements** of **incidental music** for **Dryden's play** on Sophocles' *Oedipus*, **1692**.
- The character is **Alecto**, one of the **Furies**; the music **calms her** until she drops her whip and the snakes fall from her head.
- Written for **voice (usually tenor) and continuo**; this edition is **soprano, harpsichord and bass viol**, transposed from **C minor** to **A minor**.
- The **bass viol**: six strings tuned **D, G, C, E, A, D**, flat back, sloped shoulders, **C holes**, **frets**, **underhand bow grip**.

- A **da capo aria** is foreshadowed by the reprise at **bar 29**.

questions.prompt: Describe the ground bass in *Music for a While*, and explain how Purcell keeps the music interesting despite the repetition. Refer to bars. (8 marks)
questions.solution:
The piece is built on a **ground bass**, also called a **basso ostinato** — a short recurring pattern in the bass that acts as the **principal structural element** while the parts above change. Purcell was regarded as a **master** of the device; his best-known example is *"Dido's Lament"*.

This ground is **three bars long** and consists **entirely of quaver rhythms**. Its melodic shape is **arpeggio based** and it makes use of **semitone intervals**. It has a **rising line**, starting on **A** and moving up through **B, C, D and E** before falling at the end of the phrase, where there is a characteristic **fall of an octave**.

Crucially, the ground **ends on chord V**, so it **sounds incomplete**. The sense of a **perfect cadence** is achieved only with the **chord I at the start of the next repetition** — for example bars 3 to 4, a **Ic–V–I cadential 6–4**. Because the cadence straddles the join, each ending is also a beginning, and the listener is carried forward rather than allowed to settle.

Purcell keeps the music interesting in two ways. First, **everything above the ground changes**: the vocal line is mainly **syllabic** but breaks into **melisma** at expressive moments — *"wond'ring"* at bar 10, *"eternal"* at bar 20 — and is full of **word-painting**, such as *"drop"* sung **nine times** on the weak off-beat in bars 23 to 25 as the snakes fall from Alecto's head. The **harpsichord right hand** is an **elaborate realisation**, decorated with dotted rhythms, mordents, grace notes and appoggiaturas, and provides **some counterpoint** with the voice.

Second, **the ground itself does not simply repeat**. It is heard **four and a half times in the tonic** before **beginning to modulate at bar 14**, using motifs from the original rather than the ground complete. It **returns in the original key at bar 23, beat 3**, for a **three-bar reminder**, and only **returns complete at bar 29**, where it is heard a further three times to the close. That departure and return gives the piece a large-scale shape on top of the repetition.

The sense of a **perfect cadence** is achieved only with the **chord I at the start of the next repetition** — for example bars 3 to 4, a **Ic–V–I cadential 6–4**. Because the cadence straddles the join, each ending is also a beginning, and the listener is carried forward rather than allowed to settle.

Purcell keeps the music interesting in two ways. First, **everything above the ground changes**: the vocal line is mainly **syllabic** but breaks into **melisma** at expressive moments — *"wond'ring"* at bar 10, *"eternal"* at bar 20 — and is full of **word-painting**, such as *"drop"* sung **nine times** on the weak off-beat in bars 23 to 25 as the snakes fall from Alecto's head. The **harpsichord right hand** is an **elaborate realisation**, decorated with dotted rhythms, mordents, grace notes and appoggiaturas, and provides **some counterpoint** with the voice.

Second, **the ground itself does not simply repeat**. It is heard **four and a half times in the tonic** before **beginning to modulate at bar 14**, using motifs from the original rather than the ground complete. It **returns in the original key at bar 23, beat 3**, for a **three-bar reminder**, and only **returns complete at bar 29**, where it is heard a further three times to the close. That departure and return gives the piece a large-scale shape on top of the repetition.

questions.prompt: Explain how Purcell uses word-painting in *Music for a While*, giving specific examples with the words and what the music does. (8 marks)
questions.solution:
**Word-painting** is the technique of writing music that reflects the **literal meaning** of the words being sung. Purcell uses it throughout this aria, which is set in a scene where **the music itself calms the Fury Alecto** until she drops her whip and the snakes fall from her head.

The most famous example is on the word **"drop"**, in **bars 23 to 25**. It is set in a **descending pattern**, placed on the **weak off-beat**, and sung with unusual repetition — **nine times**. The falling, halting effect directly depicts the **snakes dropping from Alecto's head**.

Purcell also uses **dissonance** to paint discomfort. On the word **"pains"** in **bar 12** there is a dissonance of **E in the melodic line against D in the bass**, so the harmony itself is painful. In the phrase **"pains were eas'd"**, bars **13 to 14**, dissonance is followed by **resolution** on the word *"eas'd"*, falling in a **descending sequence** — the music is eased exactly as the text says.

**Melisma** is used for words suggesting length or wonder. **"Wond'ring"** in **bar 10** has a wistfully **descending legato melismatic** line that captures the mood of the word, and **"eternal"** in **bar 20** is set to a **lengthy melisma with repetitive alternating notes**, suggesting something everlasting.

Purcell also paints with **key**. The phrase **"free the dead"** sits in the **bright key of G major**, bars **16 to 17**, with **rising melodies** — a moment of light in an otherwise dark piece. More broadly, the **predominantly minor key** suits the **sombre nature** of Dryden's play and the text.

Taken together, these devices show word-painting operating at every level: rhythm and contour for *"drop"*, harmony for *"pains"*, text setting for *"eternal"*, and tonality for *"free the dead"*.

questions.prompt: Why is the harpsichord right-hand part described as a realisation?
options: It was written out in full by Purcell in his own manuscript
It doubles the vocal line exactly all the way through the aria
It was added by the bass viol player during the rehearsals
The player improvised it at the time from a figured bass
questions.solution: In Baroque continuo practice the composer supplied a **bass line with figures**, and the keyboard player **improvised** the harmony above it. The elaborate, ornamented right hand printed in this edition is an editorial **realisation** of what a player would have invented.

questions.prompt: Compare how Purcell uses repetition in *Music for a While* with how a composer of a later period might structure a song. Refer to the ground bass, the tonality and the text setting, using bar numbers. (12 marks)
questions.solution:
Purcell builds the whole song on a **ground bass**: a **three-bar** pattern, **entirely in quavers** and **arpeggio based**, repeating in the **harpsichord left hand and bass viol** while everything above it changes. The repetition is therefore **structural** rather than decorative — it is the thing that holds the piece together.

Within that fixed frame Purcell finds constant variety. The **vocal line** is mainly **syllabic** but opens into **melisma** at expressive moments — *"wond'ring"* at **bar 10**, *"eternal"* at **bar 20** — and is shaped by **word-painting**, most famously *"drop"* sung **nine times** on the weak off-beat in **bars 23 to 25**. The **harpsichord right hand** is an **elaborate realisation**, decorated with dotted rhythms, mordents, grace notes and appoggiaturas, offering **some counterpoint** to the voice. And the ground itself is not rigid: it is heard **four and a half times in the tonic**, **breaks off to modulate at bar 14** using its own motifs, **returns for a three-bar reminder at bar 23 beat 3**, and only **returns complete at bar 29**.

**Tonally** the piece is in **A minor** — transposed from Purcell's **C minor** — coloured at the close by a **Tierce de Picardie**. The tonality is **sometimes ambiguous**, because the ground is **chromatic and non-diatonic**, and the central section passes through **E minor (14), G major (16), C major (21), A major (23) and E minor (27)** before returning to the tonic at **bar 28**, each modulation **confirmed by a perfect cadence**. The bass thus provides stability and instability at once.

A composer of a later period would typically organise a song quite differently. A **strophic** song repeats the **music** for each verse while the **words** change — the opposite emphasis, since the melody is the constant. A **through-composed** song refuses repetition altogether, following the text wherever it goes. Purcell sits between the two: he repeats a **bass**, not a tune, and lets the melody respond freely to the words.

He also points forward. The **reprise of opening material at bar 29**, in identical form with only a slight extension, anticipates the **ternary *da capo* aria** that became standard in later Baroque opera — a large-scale A–B–A shape laid over the ground bass technique.

The judgement is that the ground bass gives Purcell something a strophic or through-composed structure cannot: an **unbroken sense of forward motion**, because the ground ends on **chord V** and resolves only at the **next repetition**, combined with **complete freedom** in the vocal line above it. The repetition is what licenses the expressive detail, rather than constraining it.

examTechnique.body:
Describe the **ground bass** fully — three bars, all quavers, arpeggio based, semitone intervals, rising from A then falling an octave, **ending on chord V** so the cadence completes at the next repetition — and say **what changes above it**.

For word-painting, name the **word**, the **bar** and the **device**. Be precise about key: **A minor**, transposed from Purcell's **C minor**, with a **Tierce de Picardie**. There is **no tempo marking**, so quote bars, never timings.
examinerErrors: Saying the ground bass repeats unchanged throughout.
Giving the key as C minor for this edition, or A minor for Purcell’s original.
Naming word-painting without the word or the bar.
Confusing a false relation with an ordinary dissonance or a suspension.
Saying the harpsichord right hand was written out by Purcell.
Describing the texture as polyphonic rather than melody-dominated homophony.
Forgetting that the bass viol doubles the ground bass.

Word-painting comes with word, bar and device: *"drop"* nine times on the weak off-beat as the snakes fall. It distinguishes the **false relation** in bar 1 from the dissonance on *"pains"* and the 4–3 suspension in bar 3, is precise that the edition is A minor transposed from C minor with a Tierce de Picardie, and knows the right hand is an editorial realisation of an improvised continuo part.
